lines.text: Stop watching coding tutorials | if you actually want to learn to code.
I watched forty hours of them. | Then I opened an empty file, | to build something on my own. | And I *froze*.
Not one line. | If that's you, | it's not your brain. | It's the method.
Here's what's really going on, | and what fixed it for me.
First, *the freeze.* | You follow along, | the code works, | you feel great.
Then the video ends, | and so does your coding. | You learned the video, | not the skill. | People call this *tutorial hell*.
So why does watching feel like learning? | Because it's *familiar*.
You see the code | and think, | yeah, I know that. | But seeing it isn't writing it.
Recognising a face is easy. | Drawing it from memory is hard. | Coding is drawing from memory.
Scientists tested this. | One group read a passage *fourteen times*.
Another group read it about three times, | then tested themselves. | No notes. | Just recall.
One week later? | The re-readers remembered *forty percent*. | The testers, *sixty-one*.
And here's the part that stung. | The re-readers felt *more* confident.
Next. | *Write it, | don't watch it.*
A huge review of two hundred twenty-five studies | compared college science lectures | with classes where students actually did the work.
In lectures, | about thirty-four in a hundred failed. | Doing the work? | About *twenty-two*.
So watching was never the problem. | Watching *only* was. | And that's when I changed how I learn.
Quick thing. | This is exactly why I switched to Teyro.
Every lesson has me writing real code within minutes. | More on that later. | First, the part that made it stick.
*Instant feedback.* | A video can't tell you you're wrong.
So you practise the mistake | until it feels right. | You need to know in seconds, | not after the project breaks.
Then, *tiny steps.* | One idea. | Use it. | Then come back tomorrow.
In that same study, | the re-readers forgot about *half* of what they'd learned within a week. | The testers? | Just *fourteen percent*.
Pull it back out of your head again, | and it stays.
Now, *the trap.* | Five minutes after studying, | the re-readers actually scored higher.
Testing yourself feels slower. | Harder. | Like you're failing.
But that struggle is the learning. | Researchers call it a *desirable difficulty*.
To be fair, | videos aren't useless. | Watch to get the idea. | Then close it, | and write it yourself.
So. | Watching feels like knowing. | Recall beats re-reading. | Do the work. | Get feedback fast. | Small steps, | every day.
That's how I learn now, | and I do it on Teyro.
I started with the free Git, GitHub and GitHub Actions course. | Fifty-seven short lessons.
Each one takes a few minutes, | in four steps. | Learn, | apply, | reflect, | deepen.
I write real code, | and every answer gets checked instantly. | Right answers earn XP.
My streak grows every day, | and a freeze covers a busy one. | Weekly leagues, | Bronze to Diamond. | Daily quests and chests.
Friends to race, | and a course community | that cheers your wins.
And the meter flipped. | My first commit. | My first pull request. | A GitHub Action that runs on its own.
You don't learn code by watching it. | You learn it by *writing* it.
Want to actually learn to code? | Learn it on Teyro.
Search for it in your browser, | or go straight to Teyro dot app.
